stages.title: African kingdoms and empires
stages.hook: In 1324 a king travelled from West Africa to Mecca with so much gold that, according to later accounts, prices in Cairo were affected. Who was he, and where did the gold come from?
explain: West Africa's great medieval states grew rich on trade across the Sahara. Gold from the south was traded for salt, cloth and other goods from the north, carried by camel caravans. The Ghana Empire, then the Mali Empire and then the Songhai Empire controlled these routes in turn.

Mali was built up by Sundiata Keita in the 1200s. Its ruler Mansa Musa made a famous pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324 to 1325. Timbuktu became a centre of learning, with scholars, libraries and the Sankore mosque. Songhai grew in the 1400s and 1500s and fell after a Moroccan army defeated it at Tondibi in 1591.

Elsewhere, Great Zimbabwe, in southern Africa, was a stone-walled capital that traded gold with the Swahili coast. The Kingdom of Kongo in central Africa, the Benin Kingdom famous for bronze plaques, and Oyo among the Yoruba were also powerful. These were separate states with their own histories.

example.q: Why did control of the Sahara trade make a state rich?
steps: Gold lay in the south; salt and cloth were wanted there.
Merchants had to pass through the ruler's lands.
The ruler taxed the trade and protected the routes.
example.a: Taxing and protecting trade routes brought wealth.

analogies.sea: Swahili ports like Kilwa were harbours where goods from inland met ships from the Indian Ocean.
analogies.city: Timbuktu was a crossroads, like a modern airport hub for goods and ideas.
analogies.music: Griots, West African historians, keep the past in song and speech.

misc.right: Africa has Arabic and other written records, plus rich oral traditions and archaeology.

stages.limits: Documented fact: Timbuktu manuscripts and archaeology. Oral tradition: Sundiata epic. Scholarly uncertainty: details of dates and Mansa Musa's wealth.

stages.title: Medieval European societies
stages.hook: In 1347 a disease arrived by ship in Europe. Within a few years, a huge part of the population had died. How could such a thing change a whole society?
explain: Medieval Europe, roughly the years 500 to 1500, was mostly rural. Under feudalism, kings gave land to lords in return for loyalty and service, and ordinary people, many of them serfs, farmed the land. The Christian Church was powerful and ran schools, hospitals and monasteries.

From about 1000, towns, trade and craft guilds grew, and the first universities opened. In 1215, the English barons made King John seal Magna Carta, which limited royal power. Europe was not isolated: Islamic scholars, Byzantine traders and Viking explorers all linked it to other lands.

The Black Death arrived in 1347 and killed a large share of the population in a few years; estimates are a third or more. Afterwards, with fewer workers, labourers could demand better pay, and old feudal ties weakened.

example.q: Why could survivors of the plague often demand higher wages?
steps: Many workers had died.
Fewer people were left to do the same work.
Landowners needed workers, so they paid more.
example.a: Labour became scarce, so it was worth more.

analogies.farm: A manor was like a large farm where peasants worked land for a lord.
analogies.city: Guilds were like trade unions and clubs for craftspeople.
analogies.tech: Monasteries copied books by hand, much like a slow human printer.

misc.wrong: The medieval period was a dark age of no progress.
misc.right: It saw new farming methods, universities, cathedrals and trade, though with great hardships too.

stages.limits: Documented fact: Magna Carta, plague records. Scholarly uncertainty: death toll estimates vary by region and source.

stages.title: Byzantine history
stages.hook: A city sat on the strait between two continents and stayed a great capital for over a thousand years. Why was its location so powerful?
explain: The Byzantine Empire was the eastern half of the Roman Empire, which lasted after the western half fell in 476 CE. Its capital, Constantinople (today's Istanbul), was dedicated in 330 CE by Constantine. The people called themselves Romans, spoke Greek and were mostly Christian.

Constantinople stood on the Bosporus, linking Europe and Asia, and was a hub of trade by land and sea. The emperor Justinian (ruled 527 to 565) had the great church Hagia Sophia built, finished in 537, and ordered Roman law to be gathered in a code that influenced later legal systems.
The empire faced many pressures from Persians, Arabs, Bulgars and others. Constantinople fell to the Ottoman Turks in 1453, and that is usually seen as the end of the empire.

example.q: Why did Constantinople's location help it survive?
steps: It was on a strait linking two seas and two continents.
Trade passed through, making it rich.
Strong walls and sea defences made it hard to attack.
example.a: Its trade position and strong defences protected it.

analogies.city: Constantinople was like a major airport hub, connecting routes in many directions.
analogies.sea: A strait is like a narrow doorway ships must pass.
analogies.home: A family house with thick walls is safer in a storm, like the city's walls.

stages.mnemonic: 330 founded, 537 church, 1453 fell: three Byzantine dates.

misc.wrong: The Roman Empire ended completely in 476.

stages.limits: The name 'Byzantine' was used later by historians; people at the time called themselves Romans.

stages.title: Islamic civilisations and intellectual achievements
stages.hook: The word 'algebra' comes from an Arabic book title. How did mathematics from Baghdad reach the whole world?
explain: Islam began in Arabia in the 600s CE, and within about a century the caliphates governed lands from Spain to Central Asia. Under the Abbasid caliphs, Baghdad was founded in 762 and became a centre of learning. Scholars of many faiths and languages translated Greek, Persian and Indian works into Arabic and added new ideas.

Al-Khwarizmi wrote a book on solving equations whose title gave us the word algebra. Ibn al-Haytham studied how light and vision work using experiments. Ibn Sina (Avicenna) wrote the Canon of Medicine, used for centuries in Asia and Europe. Fatima al-Fihri founded the University of al-Qarawiyyin in Fez in 859. Cordoba in Spain was another great centre.
These ideas spread along trade routes. Hindu-Arabic numerals and paper-making reached Europe through the Islamic world.

example.q: How did translating books help science?
steps: Scholars gathered works from different languages.
They compared methods and tested claims.
They added new discoveries and passed the knowledge on.
example.a: Translation connected knowledge and sparked new work.

analogies.city: Baghdad was like a great modern university city.
analogies.tech: Translators were like the first search engines, bringing sources together.
analogies.sea: Merchants carried both goods and ideas across the Indian Ocean.

A branch of mathematics for solving equations.

misc.right: They preserved, challenged and extended earlier knowledge with new discoveries.

stages.title: Medieval South and East Asian empires
stages.hook: A Chinese dynasty printed books and used paper money centuries before Europe. What other firsts happened in medieval Asia?
explain: In China the Tang dynasty (618 to 907) had a great capital, Chang'an, linked to the Silk Road. The Song dynasty (960 to 1279) saw printing spread, paper money, and the use of gunpowder and the magnetic compass. In 1271 the Mongol ruler Kublai Khan founded the Yuan dynasty.

In South India, the Chola dynasty built the Brihadisvara temple around 1010 and sent ships to Southeast Asia. The Khmer Empire built Angkor Wat in the early 1100s in Cambodia. In Japan, the Heian period (794 to 1185) produced the novel The Tale of Genji by Murasaki Shikibu, and later samurai warriors gained power with the Kamakura shogunate from 1185.
These empires traded and exchanged ideas across the Indian Ocean and Silk Road.

example.q: Why was paper money practical for Song traders?
steps: Copper coins were heavy to carry in large amounts.
Paper notes were light and could be issued by authorities.
So large deals were easier.
example.a: Paper was lighter and easier than carrying coins.

analogies.sea: Chola ships carried goods across the Bay of Bengal.

stages.title: Mesoamerican and Andean civilisations
stages.hook: The Inca had no wheeled carts and no written alphabet, yet they ran an empire across the Andes. How?
explain: The Mexica (Aztec) built Tenochtitlan on an island in Lake Texcoco, traditionally founded in 1325. They farmed using chinampas, raised garden plots in the lake, and the city became a capital of an alliance of three city-states formed in 1428. Their language was Nahuatl.

The Inca Empire, called Tawantinsuyu, ruled the Andes from Cusco in the 1400s and early 1500s. They built a road system of tens of thousands of kilometres, used runners to send messages, and kept records on knotted cords called quipu. Before them, civilisations such as Chavín, Tiwanaku and Wari had also grown in the Andes.
Both regions farmed with great skill: maize, beans and squash in Mesoamerica, and potatoes, quinoa and terraces in the Andes.

example.q: How could the Inca govern without a writing system like ours?
steps: They used quipu, knotted cords, to record numbers and perhaps more.
Roads and relay runners carried messages fast.
Officials collected and stored goods in warehouses.

analogies.city: Tenochtitlan had causeways and canals, like a city of bridges.
analogies.tech: Quipu worked like a knotted spreadsheet.

stages.title: Indigenous North American histories
stages.hook: A city near today's St. Louis had a mound as large as a pyramid base nearly a thousand years ago. Who built it?
explain: North America has been home to hundreds of Indigenous nations for thousands of years. Cahokia, near modern St. Louis, was the largest Mississippian city, peaking about 1050 to 1200 CE, with Monks Mound as its largest earthwork. In the southwest, Ancestral Puebloans built cliff dwellings at Mesa Verde and great houses at Chaco Canyon.

The Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) Confederacy joined nations in a council under the Great Law of Peace; the date of its founding is debated among scholars and oral tradition. On the Pacific Northwest coast, peoples carved totem poles and held potlatches. Inuit peoples lived in the Arctic using ingenious technology to survive the cold.
These are only a few of the many nations, each with its own languages, laws and histories, handed down in oral traditions and archaeology.

example.q: Why is a confederacy a good way to unite nations?
steps: Each nation keeps its own identity.
A council makes shared decisions on common matters.
Agreement is by discussion, not by one ruler.
example.a: It joins nations while each keeps its own voice.

analogies.city: Cahokia's plazas and mounds were the centre of a busy city.
analogies.sea: Totem poles on the coast told family histories.
analogies.nature: Ancestral Puebloan homes in cliffs used the rock for shelter.

stages.title: Australian and Pacific maritime traditions
stages.hook: In 1976 a canoe sailed from Hawaii to Tahiti using no maps or instruments. How could a crew navigate such a distance?
explain: Pacific peoples explored the largest ocean on Earth in double-hulled and outrigger canoes. Navigators learned the star paths, the direction of ocean swells and the flight of birds. Polynesians settled a huge triangle from Hawaii to Aotearoa (New Zealand) to Rapa Nui. In 1976 the canoe Hokule'a sailed from Hawaii to Tahiti, guided by the navigator Mau Piailug from Satawal in Micronesia, to show these methods work.

In the Marshall Islands, navigators made stick charts of woven palm ribs to represent swells. In northern Australia, Yolngu people had contact with Makassan traders from Sulawesi for centuries before British settlement, trading for trepang.
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples also have sea-country knowledge, with stories and laws about reefs, tides and fishing.

example.q: How can swells help a navigator?
steps: Swells bend around islands and create patterns.
A navigator feels them in the canoe.
The pattern shows where land lies, even out of sight.
example.a: Swell patterns reveal land beyond the horizon.

analogies.sea: Reading the ocean is like reading a map written in motion.
analogies.nature: Birds that roost on land show which way to sail at dusk.
analogies.music: Navigators learned star paths as songs and chants.

stages.mnemonic: Stars, swells, birds, sticks: four tools of Pacific navigators.
terms: A canoe with a float attached to one side for stability.
A map of swells made of sticks and shells.
Sea cucumber, traded in northern Australia.

misc.wrong: Pacific islands were settled by accident, by drifting.
misc.right: Evidence shows deliberate voyaging with navigation skill.

stages.limits: Documented fact: Hokule'a voyage 1976, archaeological dates. Scholarly uncertainty: exact settlement dates of some islands.

stages.title: Intercontinental trade and cultural exchange
stages.hook: A traveller from Morocco, Ibn Battuta, journeyed for about thirty years and visited lands from Mali to China. What did people exchange along the way?
explain: Long before modern transport, trade networks linked continents. The Silk Road carried silk, paper, spices and ideas across Asia. The Indian Ocean monsoon winds allowed sailors to cross between East Africa, Arabia, India and Southeast Asia. Trans-Saharan caravans carried gold and salt.

Travellers wrote about what they saw. Ibn Battuta (about 1304 to 1368 or 1369) visited many lands. Marco Polo, from Venice, travelled to the Mongol court in the late 1200s. Zheng He led large Chinese fleets across the Indian Ocean from 1405 to 1433.
Exchange was not only goods. Religions such as Buddhism and Islam spread, numerals and paper moved west, and unfortunately diseases like the Black Death also travelled these routes.

example.q: Why were monsoon winds useful for sailors?
steps: They blow one way in one season and the opposite way in another.
Sailors could travel out with one and return with the other.
So regular sea trade was predictable.
example.a: The seasonal reversal made round trips reliable.

analogies.sea: The monsoon was like a seasonal conveyor belt for ships.
analogies.city: A port city is like a market where the world meets.
analogies.tech: Trade routes were the early internet, carrying goods and ideas.

stages.mnemonic: Silk by land, spice by sea, gold by camel.
terms: A seasonal wind that reverses direction.
A group travelling together, often with camels.
The sharing of ideas, arts and customs between peoples.
People settled away from their original homeland.

misc.right: Trade also moved religions, ideas, technologies, foods and diseases.

stages.limits: Documented fact: routes and travel accounts. Scholarly uncertainty: details in Marco Polo's account are debated.

teach.model: Trade networks like the Silk Road, the Indian Ocean routes and the Sahara caravans linked continents. They carried goods, religions, ideas and also diseases, so contact brought both benefits and problems.
